# Climate Policy Radar

> An open database of the world's climate law, policy, litigation, climate
> finance and UN Convention submissions, with full text, expert concept
> labelling and provenance. Maintained by Climate Policy Radar CIC, a
> non-profit.

Use this API when you need the *primary source text* of national climate laws,
policies, NDCs, court cases or fund documents — not summaries of them. Coverage
is global and multilingual; documents are stored in their original language with
English translations of matching passages available.

## Data model

Understanding these four concepts is necessary to query the API well.

- **Document** — one published item (a law, a policy, a court filing, an NDC).
  Has `id`, `title`, `description`, an `attributes` bag of metadata, and
  relationships to other documents.
- **Document relationships** — documents are connected to each other via
  `documents[].value`. The edge of those nodes is described by `documents[].type`.
- **Passage** — a text block within a document, produced by the PDF/HTML layout
  parser. Carries `text`, `language`, page numbers and bounding-box coordinates
  so a match can be located precisely on the page. `idx` gives reading order.
  Passages are the right granularity for evidence and citation; documents are
  the right granularity for "does this country have X".
- **Label** (also called **Concept**, and marketed as **Topics**) — an
  expert-curated concept such as "adaptation finance" or "just transition".
  A Label is *not* a keyword: it packages `alternative_labels` (synonyms),
  `subconcept_labels` (narrower terms), `negative_labels` (exclusions) and
  regional variations. Searching by Label rather than by string is how you avoid
  missing "increasing climate resilience" when you searched "climate adaptation".
  There are 100+ Labels. Prefer Label filtering over keyword queries for recall.
  Label filtering can also affect `Document` and `Passage` ranking.

## Querying

Every path below is relative to `https://api.climatepolicyradar.org`, so
`/search/documents` is `https://api.climatepolicyradar.org/search/documents`.
No authentication — see Limits and etiquette.

- `GET /search/documents` — search and filter documents.
- `GET /search/documents/{document_id}` — retrieve one document.
- `GET /search/passages` — search passage text. Defaults to `idx asc` (reading
  order); pass `order_by=relevance desc` for best-match-first.
- `GET /search/labels` — look up available Labels/Topics by name or type.
- `GET /search/labels-taxonomy` — the Label hierarchy.

Shared parameters: `query`, `filters`, `order_by`, `page_token`, `page_size`.

`query` runs exclusively on lexical search.

`GET /search/openapi.json` is the machine-readable contract for all of the
above — exact response shapes, enum values and parameter types. Read it when
you need the precise schema of a response; read this file for how the pieces
fit together and which query to reach for. The two are complementary, and the
OpenAPI schema is generated from the running service, so where they disagree
it is right about shapes and this file is right about meaning. Browsable docs
are at `/search/docs`.

### `filters`

`filters` takes a URL-encoded JSON *filter tree*. The top level is always a
group:

```json
{"op": "and", "filters": [ ...conditions or nested groups... ]}
```

`op` is `and` or `or`; members are either further groups (nesting is
unlimited) or conditions. There is no top-level `not` — negate the individual
condition instead. A filter is ANDed with `query` rather than replacing it, and
the same filter is applied to any `aggregations`/`facets` you request
alongside the results.

**Field conditions** match an indexed field:

```json
{"field": "labels.value.id", "op": "contains", "value": "geography::USA"}
```

`op` is `contains` or `not_contains`; `value` is a string, number or boolean.
`contains` is index matching, not substring matching.

**Attribute conditions** match one key inside a document's `attributes` bag,
and are the only way to use an ordering operator:

```json
{"field": "attributes_double", "key": "project_cost_usd", "op": "gte", "value": 1000000}
```

`field` names the typed map to look in — `attributes_string`,
`attributes_double`, `attributes_boolean`, `attributes_identifiers`, or the
special-cased `attributes.published_date`. `op` is `eq`, `not_eq`, `lt`, `lte`,
`gt` or `gte`; the four ordering operators are numeric- and date-only and are
rejected on `attributes_string`.

`{"field": "attributes.<key>", "op": "contains", "value": ...}` is a shorthand
field condition for the same lookup: the JSON type of `value` picks the map
(string → `attributes_string`, number → `attributes_double`, boolean →
`attributes_boolean`). It cannot reach `attributes_identifiers` and cannot
express a range; use the long form for those.

### Filterable fields

`/documents`

- `labels.value.id` — a Label id, always `{type}::{name}`: `geography::USA`,
  `category::Law`, `topic::Adaptation`, `concept::Q1343`.
- `labels.value.value` — the Label's display string, e.g. `Romania`.
- `labels.type` — the *relationship* between document and Label, not the
  Label's own type.
- `id`, `title`, `description`, `geographies` — indexed document fields.
- `attributes.*` — as above.

`/passages`

- `document_id`, `principal_id`.
- `labels.value.id`, `labels.value.value`, `labels.value.type`.

`/labels`

- `labels.type`, `labels.value.id`, `labels.value.value`, `labels.value.type` —
  these filter a Label's relationships to *other* Labels, which is how you walk
  the taxonomy.

Field names outside these lists are passed to the index unchanged rather than
rejected at the boundary, so a typo surfaces as a backend error and not a
`400`. Malformed filter JSON, an unrecognised `op`, and a non-ISO-8601
`published_date` are all `400`.

### Same-element matching on passages and labels

On `/passages` and `/labels`, `labels` is an array of structs, and `labels.*`
conditions ANDed *inside one group* must all be satisfied by the **same** array
element. Two different ids ANDed in one group therefore match nothing. To
require two different Labels on the same passage, give each its own group:

```json
{"op": "and", "filters": [
  {"op": "and", "filters": [
    {"field": "labels.value.id", "op": "contains", "value": "concept::Q1343"}]},
  {"op": "and", "filters": [
    {"field": "labels.value.id", "op": "contains", "value": "concept::Q7987"}]}]}
```

Same-element matching is what you want when the conditions describe one Label:
`labels.type` and `labels.value.id` in a single group pin the relationship and
its target together. `/documents` does no array-struct filtering, so its label
conditions are always independent of one another.

### Worked examples

Documents for a geography — URL-encode the JSON in a real request:

```
GET /search/documents?filters={"op":"and","filters":[{"field":"labels.value.id","op":"contains","value":"geography::USA"}]}
```

Documents published in a closed date range. `published_date` is stored as a
Unix timestamp; ISO-8601 strings are converted at the boundary, and `key` must
be `published_date`:

```json
{"op": "and", "filters": [
  {"field": "attributes.published_date", "key": "published_date",
   "op": "gte", "value": "2019-01-01T00:00:00Z"},
  {"field": "attributes.published_date", "key": "published_date",
   "op": "lte", "value": "2023-12-31T23:59:59Z"}]}
```

A Label query using all three combinators — US laws or policies, excluding one
concept:

```json
{"op": "and", "filters": [
  {"op": "or", "filters": [
    {"field": "labels.value.id", "op": "contains", "value": "category::Law"},
    {"field": "labels.value.id", "op": "contains", "value": "category::Policy"}]},
  {"field": "labels.value.id", "op": "contains", "value": "geography::USA"},
  {"field": "labels.value.id", "op": "not_contains", "value": "concept::Q1343"}]}
```

Filtering `/documents` by a `concept::` Label also affects ranking: when you
order by `relevance`, matching documents are reordered by how often they
mention that concept, so the most substantive treatment comes first. An
explicit `order_by` on any other field disables that reordering, and
`not_contains` never contributes to it — excluding a concept must not boost it.

`order_by` takes comma-separated `<field> <direction>` clauses (AIP-132).
Documents support `relevance`, `attributes.published_date`, `title`. Passages
support `relevance`, `idx`.

### Dates

`published_date` is the only date-typed key in `attributes`. It arrives as an
ISO-8601 string and is stored twice: verbatim in `attributes_string`, and as
epoch seconds in a scalar field that backs both date comparison and date sort.

Compare against it with the long-form attribute condition, which targets the
scalar:

```json
{"field": "attributes.published_date", "key": "published_date",
 "op": "gte", "value": "2019-01-01T00:00:00Z"}
```

`key` must be `published_date`. `value` is either an ISO-8601 string —
converted to epoch seconds at the boundary, with a non-ISO string rejected as a
`400` — or an epoch-seconds integer, which is passed through untouched. Always
include `Z` or an explicit offset: a naive datetime is resolved against the
server's local timezone rather than UTC.

The `{"field": "attributes.published_date", "op": "contains", ...}` shorthand
does something different, and quietly. `contains` is not an attribute-condition
operator, so the condition parses as a field condition and string-matches the
stored ISO text in `attributes_string`. It cannot express a range, and it will
miss a date written with a different offset or precision to the stored one. Use
the long form for anything involving dates.

Undated documents — no `published_date`, or one that failed to parse at feed
time — have no scalar value at all. They are excluded by every date filter, and
sorted last by `order_by=attributes.published_date` in both directions. Only
the first `order_by` clause is applied.

The rest of the `attributes` bag varies by corpus and is not enumerated here.

## Recommended query strategy

1. Resolve the user's concept to a Label via `/search/labels` before searching.
   Free-text queries under-recall badly on this corpus because the same policy
   idea is phrased differently across jurisdictions and languages.
2. Use `/search/documents` with Label filters to establish *which* documents are
   relevant, then `/search/passages` to extract quotable evidence.
3. Check `documents[].type` relationships before asserting that a law is current.
4. Cite the document `id` and passage page number; both are stable.

## Limits and etiquette

No authentication. There is no API key and no auth header — every endpoint is
open, and any origin may call it. Please be proportionate with request volume:
this is a non-profit's infrastructure, and the bulk dataset below is the right
tool for anything resembling a full crawl.

**Paginate on the request, not the response.** `page_token` (1-based) and
`page_size` work as offset and limit. The `page`, `page_size`, `total_pages`,
`next_page` and `previous_page` fields *in the response* are not yet
implemented: they are always `0` or `null` whatever the result set. Do not
iterate by following `next_page` — you will read the first page and conclude
you have everything. Instead increment `page_token` yourself, and stop when a
page returns fewer than `page_size` results or when you have covered
`total_size`, which is the one pagination field that carries a real value.

The API enforces no `page_size` ceiling of its own. The effective limits are
the index's — 50,001 hits, 500,000 offset — and a 5-second query timeout;
exceeding any of them surfaces as a `503`. Note that the timeout degrades
rather than fails: a query that runs out of budget returns whatever it had
found so far, with a `200`, so results under heavy load can be incomplete
without saying so.

The corpus is rebuilt daily. Documents, passages and Labels are all
re-materialised and fed overnight, so expect the index to be at most a day
behind the upstream sources.
